items.description: Self-hosted observability: metrics, logs, traces, dashboards and alerts. Stores data in PostgreSQL or ClickHouse. Accepts OpenTelemetry data.
items.readme:
# DataCat

Self-hosted observability: metrics, logs, distributed traces, dashboards, infrastructure
and alerts in one place. DataCat runs on your infrastructure, stores data in PostgreSQL (or telemetry in
ClickHouse, if you choose; see docs/SELF_HOSTING.md), and accepts OpenTelemetry and Datadog-compatible agent traffic.
No hosted account or external service is required.

## Features

- Metrics explorer, formulas, dashboards and host maps
- Searchable logs with facets, live tail and trace correlation
- APM service catalog, trace explorer and waterfall
- Metric, log and trace monitors with webhook/Slack notifications
- Organizations, local accounts, single-use invites, API/application keys
- OpenTelemetry Collector-based host agent and Node.js/Python instrumentation libraries
- One production process serving the API, web UI, installer and downloads

![DataCat dashboard](docs/images/dashboard.jpg)

## Quick start with Docker Compose

Requirements: Docker Engine with the Compose plugin, Git, and OpenSSL.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/replit/datacat
cd datacat
cp .env.example .env
sed -i "s/^POSTGRES_PASSWORD=.*/POSTGRES_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -hex 24)/" .env
sed -i "s/^SESSION_SECRET=.*/SESSION_SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 32)/" .env
chmod 600 .env
mkdir -p downloads
docker compose up -d --build
```

Open **http://localhost:3000**, create your admin account and organization, then create
an API key under **Organization Settings**. Setup asks for a setup token, printed in the
server log (`docker compose logs datacat | grep "setup token"`) unless you set `DATACAT_SETUP_TOKEN`.
Set `PUBLIC_URL` to your externally reachable HTTPS origin before inviting colleagues or
installing agents remotely.

Agent binaries and SDK packages are separate release assets. Put them (including
`SHA256SUMS`) in `downloads/` to serve them from your instance.

## Sending data

DataCat accepts the Datadog public intake API and OTLP/HTTP:

| Sender | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Datadog Agent 7.56.2 (metrics, logs, check runs, traces) | Tested in CI-style runs |
| Datadog Agent 7.85.4 (metrics, logs, check runs, traces) | Tested with captured payloads; including the newer string-table trace format |
| Datadog Agent 7.57–7.84 | Not tested individually. Agents that send traces in a format DataCat cannot read get a 422, never a silent 202 |
| OpenTelemetry Collector / SDKs (OTLP/HTTP) | `/v1/traces`, `/v1/metrics`, `/v1/logs` (also under `/otlp/v1/*`) |
| DataCat Agent and libraries | Tested in CI |

`GET /api/v1/intake/stats` shows, per intake path, how many items were stored and how many were dropped since the
server started.

Sign-in uses local email/password accounts; members join through single-use invite links.

## From source

Use Node.js **22.15+**, pnpm **10.11.0** and PostgreSQL **14+**. Node 22 also meets
the Node SDK requirement; older Node 20 releases are not supported by the current SDK.

```sh
corepack enable
corepack prepare pnpm@10.11.0 --activate
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
BASE_PATH=/ pnpm run build:selfhost
# Set DATABASE_URL, SESSION_SECRET and PUBLIC_URL in your environment.
NODE_ENV=production PORT=3000 pnpm start
```

The server migrates its schema automatically before listening. There is no manual
schema push and no separate frontend server.

See **[Self-hosting](docs/SELF_HOSTING.md)** for clean Ubuntu installation, all environment
settings, backups, systemd, agent installation, Node/Python instrumentation and a
webhook monitor walkthrough.

## Development

```sh
pnpm run typecheck:libs
pnpm --filter @workspace/api-server run dev
# In another terminal:
API_PROXY=http://localhost:3000 PORT=5173 pnpm --filter @workspace/web run dev
```

The API needs `DATABASE_URL`; use a separate development database.
The agent is built with Go 1.26.11+:

```sh
bash agent/build.sh
DESTDIR="$PWD/dist/downloads" bash agent/release.sh
```

Tests:

```sh
pnpm --filter @workspace/api-server test     # server unit tests
DATACAT_URL=http://localhost:3000 DATACAT_SETUP_TOKEN=<token> bash scripts/e2e.sh   # end-to-end known-answer checks against a fresh install
```

CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) runs typechecks, unit tests, dependency and vulnerability audits, the end-to-end
checks on both storage options, the library and agent tests, a Docker build and a secrets scan on every pull request.

Runnable examples are in [`examples/`](examples). See [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md), [Security](SECURITY.md) and the [Changelog](CHANGELOG.md).

## Benchmarks

`bench/kit` sends metrics, logs and traces through DataCat and checks every answer against a known value; it reports
throughput, query latency and how long data takes to become searchable, for both storage options. The other folders
in [`bench/`](bench) hold the correctness, resilience, alerting, soak and isolation tests; raw results behind the
published numbers are in [`bench/evidence/`](bench/evidence).

## License

[Apache License 2.0](LICENSE). Third-party dependencies retain their own licenses.
DataCat is an independent project, not affiliated with or endorsed by Datadog, Inc. Datadog is a trademark of
Datadog, Inc.; it is named here only to describe protocol compatibility.

items.readme:
# sprite-stacking

An agent skill that turns four pixel art views into fake-3D sprites you can spin. By Daniel White.

![MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/licence-MIT-111?style=flat-square)
![Agent skill](https://img.shields.io/badge/agent-skill-111?style=flat-square)
![Python 3 + Pillow + NumPy](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python%203-Pillow%20%2B%20NumPy-111?style=flat-square)
![Works with](https://img.shields.io/badge/works%20with-Claude%20Code%20%C2%B7%20Codex%20%C2%B7%20Cursor%20%C2%B7%20OpenCode%20%C2%B7%20Gemini%20CLI%20%C2%B7%20Pi-111?style=flat-square)

![Six sprite-stacked assets spinning](media/showcase.gif)

## Install

```bash
npx skills add danielwh2/sprite-stacking
```

Installs to the current project. Add `-g` for every project, `-a claude-code` (or `codex`, `cursor`, ...) to pick an agent. Uses the [skills CLI](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills), Node 22.20 or later.

Or copy `skills/sprite-stacking` into your agent's skills folder:

| Agent | Folder |
| --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `~/.claude/skills/` |
| Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Pi | `~/.agents/skills/` |

## Use

Ask your agent:

- "Make a rotatable pixel art car."
- "Sprite stack this 4-view sheet and give me a turntable."
- "Add a fake 3D pixel art tree to my Godot game."

No image generator? The agent draws the views itself in a short Python script.

## How it works

![Sheet to slices to render](media/pipeline.png)

1. **Views:** top, side, front and back, orthographic, one row.
2. **Carve:** a voxel survives only where all four views cover it.
3. **Slices:** the volume is cut into a strip of flat layers, ground first.
4. **Render:** each layer is rotated, squashed for pitch and lifted 1 px.

## Slicer CLI

```bash
python3 skills/sprite-stacking/scripts/views_to_slices.py views.png slices.png \
  --slices 36 --preview check.png --html viewer.html
```

- `--slices N`: layer count. 15-20 chunky, 32-48 detailed.
- `--order reading`: force TOP, SIDE, FRONT, BACK. Default matches views by proportion.
- `--round`: towers, balloons, pots carve round, not square.
- `--side-nose right`: the side view faces right.
- `--colours N`: shared palette size, `0` keeps every colour.
- `--normals path.png`: save a matching 3D normal-map slice strip.
- `--emissive path.png`: save an auto-detected emissive mask strip (headlights, windows, neon).

## Viewer

`--html` writes a standalone page:
- **Modes:** Turntable, **Scene** (Living Diorama with **Neon Street** and **Meadow Island** procedural stacked props, unified Y-sorting, and multi-PNG drop / `+ Add Prop`), Slice scan, Exploded view, and **Play** mode (**Drive** with WASD/arrows + drift across infinite Street/Meadow/Grid worlds, **Wind** sway, **Shatter** & rebuild).
- **Lighting & Weather:** Live **Time of Day** (Day → Sunset → Night with auto-emissive glow and ground light pools), draggable sun (`Shift+drag`) with projected 3D shadows, and **Weather** (**Rain** with pixel streaks, ground ripples, and wavy upside-down wet reflections; **Snow** with real-time snow cap accumulation on upward-facing voxels via `normZ`).
- **Performance:** Vectorized NumPy carving, zero-allocation typed-array software rasterizer, and angle/lighting-keyed prop sprite caching (~0.2–1.5 ms/frame in Chrome).
- **Export:** 16-direction baked PNG sprite sheet export. `skills/sprite-stacking/scripts/viewer.html` also opens on its own and accepts dropped slice strips.

## Requirements

Python 3 with Pillow and NumPy (`pip install pillow numpy`).

## Contributing

```bash
python3 tests/check.py
```

Prints `ok`.

## Prior art

Sprite stacking is a long-standing indie game technique, not invented here. This skill adds the four-view carving and the agent workflow.

## Licence

MIT

items.description: Mirror of Levent Alpöge's Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis (with Claude). All credit to Levent Alpöge. Source: alpo.ge
items.readme:
# Riemann Hypothesis in Lean — by Levent Alpöge (with Claude)

> **The proof in this repository is the work of [Levent Alpöge](https://alpo.ge/).**
> On 2026-11-20 he announced that, working with Claude, he had found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis that extends to the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (for Dirichlet L-functions), and that the argument is fully formalized in Lean without assumptions.
> All credit belongs to Levent Alpöge (and Claude). This repository is an unmodified mirror of the Lean code he published, put on GitHub so that people and agents can browse, clone and check it.
>
> 本仓库只是镜像：证明由数学家 Levent Alpöge（和 Claude 合作）完成，署名与一切功劳归他。代码原样搬运，没有改动。

- Announcement (4 pages): https://alpo.ge/remark.pdf
- Original download: https://alpo.ge/lean.tar.gz.part01 … https://alpo.ge/lean.tar.gz.part14
- Merged archive in this repo's [Releases](https://github.com/CocoSgt/riemann-hypothesis-lean/releases/tag/v2026-11-20)

**Status.** As of mirroring (2026-11-20), no independent build or review of this code has been published. Treat it as a claimed proof until it has been compiled and checked.

---

## What is proved

The target statements are short. Read these two files first.

`src/Main.lean`

```lean
import Statements
import Supplements.Kernels.MainTheoremsAll

theorem riemannHypothesis : RiemannHypothesis := rhOfAll

theorem riemannZeta_eq_zero_re : RiemannZetaZerosOnLine := rhOfAll

theorem LFunction_ne_zero_of_half_lt_re : DirichletLNonvanishingRightOfHalf := allChi

theorem LFunction_eq_zero_re : DirichletLZerosOnLine := claimAll.2.1

theorem LFunction_eq_zero_re_of_isPrimitive : PrimitiveDirichletLZerosOnLine := critAll
```

- `RiemannHypothesis` is **Mathlib's own definition** (`Mathlib/NumberTheory/LSeries/RiemannZeta.lean`, line 185 at the pinned commit), so the headline statement comes from Mathlib, outside this repository:

  ```lean
  def RiemannHypothesis : Prop :=
    ∀ (s : ℂ) (_ : riemannZeta s = 0) (_ : ¬∃ n : ℕ, s = -2 * (n + 1)) (_ : s ≠ 1), s.re = 1 / 2
  ```
- `src/Statements.lean` (16 lines, imports only Mathlib) defines the other four statements:
  - `RiemannZetaZerosOnLine`: every zero of `riemannZeta` other than the trivial zeros `-2(n+1)` and `s = 1` has real part `1/2`
  - `DirichletLNonvanishingRightOfHalf`: for every Dirichlet character `χ` mod `N`, `LFunction χ s ≠ 0` when `Re s > 1/2` (excluding `χ = 1, s = 1`)
  - `DirichletLZerosOnLine` / `PrimitiveDirichletLZerosOnLine`: zeros of Dirichlet L-functions in the critical strip lie on `Re s = 1/2` (GRH for Dirichlet L-functions)
- The proof terms come from `src/Supplements/Kernels/MainTheorems.lean`:
  `allChi := UpperTheory.FinalTheorems.everyCharacter`, `rhOfAll := Formalism.VW.rh_of_every allChi`, `critAll`, `claimAll`.

## Repository layout

| Path | `.lean` files | Lines |
|---|---:|---:|
| `src/Development/` | 141,928 | 12.2 M |
| `src/Formalism/` | 18,254 | 3.2 M |
| `src/GroundTheory/` | 8,507 | 1.1 M |
| `src/ReciprocityTheory/` | 3,845 | 563 K |
| `src/CompanionTheory/` | 2,027 | 194 K |
| `src/PositivityTheory/` | 449 | 55 K |
| `src/Lemmata/` | 167 | 9 K |
| `src/Supplements/` | 3 | 22 |
| `src/BuildAid/` | 5 | 20 |
| `src/Statements.lean`, `src/Main.lean` | 2 | — |
| **Total** | **175,187** | **≈ 17.4 M** |

- `lean-toolchain`: `leanprover/lean4:v4.33.1`
- `lakefile.toml`: package `tree`, `srcDir = "src"`, Mathlib pinned at `0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474`, global options `maxHeartbeats = 4000000`, `autoImplicit = false`, extra arg `--tstack=400000`
- Libraries (`lean_lib`): `BuildAid`, `CompanionTheory`, `Development`, `Formalism`, `GroundTheory`, `GroundTheoryFields` (`GroundTheory.LocalFields` / `GlobalFields`), `Lemmata`, `PositivityTheory`, `ReciprocityTheory`, `Supplements`, `Main` (roots `Statements`, `Main`)
- `src/BuildAid/*.lean` only add namespaces to Lean's library-suggestion deny list; they contain no mathematics.

## Getting the code

Pick one.

**A. Clone this repository** (about 234 MB packed, 1.3 GB checked out):

```bash
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/CocoSgt/riemann-hypothesis-lean.git
cd riemann-hypothesis-lean
```

**B. Download the merged archive from Releases and verify it:**

```bash
curl -LO https://github.com/CocoSgt/riemann-hypothesis-lean/releases/download/v2026-11-20/lean.tar.gz
shasum -a 256 lean.tar.gz
# expect 9631b4f020199e580ba86178cb56c6e9b09f690c2369a80dc4334aa93f49c7fc  (239,275,554 bytes)
tar -xzf lean.tar.gz && cd lean
```

**C. Use the author's original parts** (most trustworthy source):

```bash
for i in $(seq -w 1 14); do curl -LO https://alpo.ge/lean.tar.gz.part$i; done
cat lean.tar.gz.part{01..14} > lean.tar.gz
shasum -a 256 lean.tar.gz   # same hash as above
tar -xzf lean.tar.gz && cd lean
```

The `src/` tree in this repository is byte-for-byte the content of that archive; this README, `.gitignore` and nothing else were added.

## Building

```bash
# 1. Install elan (Lean version manager) if needed
curl https://elan.lean-lang.org/elan-init.sh -sSf | sh -s -- -y
source ~/.elan/env

# 2. Fetch dependencies and the prebuilt Mathlib cache
lake exe cache get     # lake-manifest.json already pins Mathlib and every dependency

# 3. Build the statements first (fast sanity check), then everything
lake build Statements
lake build Main        # builds the full dependency tree of the main theorems
```

Notes:

- This is a very large build (≈ 17 M lines on top of Mathlib). No build time or memory figures have been published yet; use a machine with many cores and plenty of RAM, and expect it to run for a long time.
- `lake build` with no target builds every library in `defaultTargets`, which is more than `Main` needs.

## Checking the proof

After `lake build Main` succeeds:

**1. Axioms used by the main theorems.** Create `Check.lean` in the project root:

```lean
import Main

#print axioms riemannHypothesis
#print axioms riemannZeta_eq_zero_re
#print axioms LFunction_eq_zero_re_of_isPrimitive
```

```bash
lake env lean Check.lean
```

A clean result lists only Lean's standard axioms: `propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`. Anything else (`sorryAx`, `Lean.ofReduceBool`, a custom `axiom`) means the proof depends on something unproved.

**2. Statement review.** Confirm that `RiemannHypothesis` is Mathlib's definition at the pinned commit and that the four definitions in `src/Statements.lean` say what their names claim.

**3. Independent kernel replay (recommended).** Re-check the compiled environment with an external checker such as [`lean4checker`](https://github.com/leanprover/lean4checker), so the result does not depend on the elaborator or on any metaprogram in the repository.

**Static scan done at mirroring time** (text search over all 175,187 files, not a substitute for the steps above):

| Pattern | Files |
|---|---:|
| `sorry` | 0 |
| `admit` | 0 |
| `axiom` declarations | 0 |
| `native_decide` | 0 |
| `unsafe`, `implemented_by`, `@[extern]`, `opaque` | 0 |
| `set_option maxHeartbeats 0` | 4 |
| custom `macro` / `elab` / `syntax` | 22 (tactic shorthands) |
| `addDecl` | 1 (`Formalism/HermitianCurvature/HermitianCurvatureProofs/CutCptCopy.lean`, a command that copies existing declarations under new names; `addDecl` still goes through the kernel) |

## For agents: suggested procedure

1. Read `src/Statements.lean` and `src/Main.lean`; look up `RiemannHypothesis` in Mathlib at commit `0df444a3…`.
2. Get the code (option C if you need to trust the source, A or B for speed) and verify the SHA-256.
3. `lake exe cache get`, then `lake build Statements`, then `lake build Main`. Log time and peak memory.
4. Run `#print axioms` on the five theorems in `Main.lean`; report the exact output.
5. Optionally replay with `lean4checker`.
6. To understand the argument, follow the proof terms downward: `Supplements/Kernels/MainTheorems.lean` → `Formalism.VW.rh_of_every` and `UpperTheory.FinalTheorems.everyCharacter` (search with `grep -rn "theorem rh_of_every\|everyCharacter" src`). The author's own outline of the ideas (Stepanov-style multiplicity via chains of theta lifts of length about √X, Iwasawa towers, Rallis seesaw, Bost slope inequality, …) is in [remark.pdf](https://alpo.ge/remark.pdf).
7. Report results to the community with the commit hash, toolchain and machine details.

## Credit and license

The mathematics and the Lean code are by **Levent Alpöge**, working with Claude. The original archive was published at https://alpo.ge/ without a stated license; this mirror adds no license of its own and claims no authorship. If the author asks for this mirror to be changed or removed, it will be.

items.title: AFK-surf/xnulinux
items.description: XNU as a loadable kernel module inside Linux (macOS personality for arm64 Linux)
items.readme:
# xnulinux

Run macOS userspace on Linux by loading the macOS kernel into it.

xnulinux builds XNU, the open-source kernel of macOS, from Apple's published sources and runs it as a loadable kernel
module (`xnu.ko`) inside an unmodified arm64 Linux kernel. The hosted XNU drives the CPU and MMU directly, so macOS
processes run natively next to Linux processes on the same CPUs, with no hypervisor between them. Linux lends XNU its
memory, timers, files, network and GPU through a small interface module (`fki.ko`).

With a stock Ubuntu kernel, `insmod xnu.ko` boots a macOS 27 system disk made by Apple's own installer to the
desktop: loginwindow, WindowServer, Dock, Finder, Safari and Chrome.

![macOS and Linux userspace side by side](docs/images/macos-and-linux.jpg)

*One system, two userspaces. Left: a Terminal in the hosted macOS 27.2.1 (`sw_vers`, the Darwin kernel, launchd,
WindowServer, Dock and Finder running). Right: from that macOS, an SSH session into the Linux it runs inside (Ubuntu,
Linux 7.0, the `xnu` and `fki` modules loaded, and the `insmod xnu.ko` process the macOS kernel runs in).
Straight from the hosted framebuffer, 1280×800.*

![The hosted macOS desktop](docs/images/desktop.jpg)

*The hosted desktop at the end of a 30-minute stress run, rendered on the CPU (no GPU bridge).*

| | |
|---|---|
| ![Safari on Wikipedia's XNU article](docs/images/safari-xnu.jpg) | ![Safari on kernel.org](docs/images/safari-kernel-org.jpg) |
| ![Safari on GitHub](docs/images/safari-github.jpg) | |

*Safari in the hosted macOS: Wikipedia's article on XNU, kernel.org and the Linux repository on GitHub, over the
hosted system's network link through Linux, with the GPU bridge on (`GPU=auto`).*

## How it works

```
 macOS processes (launchd, WindowServer, Safari...)    Linux processes (systemd, sshd, xnudrmd...)
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────    ────────────────────────────────────────────
 XNU (source-built, LINUX64 machine layer, kexts)  │
   ↕ linux64 host calls (xnu-patches/include/linux64_abi.h)
 xnu.ko   (APSL side: loads and runs the kernel collection)
   ↕ FKI, the foreign kernel interface (fki_*)
 fki.ko   (GPL side: CPUs, memory, faults, IPIs, files, network, host calls)
 Linux kernel (stock distro kernel, 4K pages, PAC)
```

- **CPUs**: each hosted CPU is a Linux kernel thread pinned to a Linux CPU. XNU runs on it until it calls the host
  (idle, I/O, a timer); Linux keeps its own exception vectors, and `fki.ko` forwards the faults and user exceptions of
  XNU code to XNU's handlers.
- **Memory**: XNU gets one physically contiguous block from Linux (CMA) and manages it with its own pmap; XNU and Linux
  share the user half of the address space layout (4K pages).
- **Devices**: kexts in `kexts/` give macOS a disk (a file on the Linux side), a display (a framebuffer Linux reads), a
  keyboard and pointer, an Ethernet link (a Linux network interface), a keystore and a GPU bridge.
- **GPU**: Metal in the hosted macOS runs on `gpu/xnu-cpu-metal` (metal2vulkan over Vulkan). Vulkan reaches the Linux
  host's GPU through the DRM bridge (`kexts/XnuDrm` → host call → `gpu/xnu-drm/xnudrmd` → the Linux render node), using
  Mesa's Venus driver; without a GPU it falls back to Mesa lavapipe on the CPU.

## Status

Working, on an Apple Silicon Mac running an arm64 Linux VM (krunkit) with 1 to 6 hosted CPUs:

- macOS 27.2.1 boots to the desktop with auto-login in 31–48 s (an Apple Virtualization macOS VM on the same Mac: 49 s).
- Apps open and quit, Spotlight and the file system work; a 30-minute stress run (40 rounds of Safari, Notes,
  Calculator, TextEdit, System Settings, Spotlight and a disk walk) finishes with no panic and no crash report.
- Runs as a systemd service: started at boot, stopped cleanly with the VM, restarted after a hosted-kernel panic, each
  run's log kept in `/var/log/xnulinux/`.
- The GPU bridge gives hosted apps the host GPU (`Virtio-GPU Venus (Apple M5 Max)`) and is enabled by default
  (`GPU=auto`) when a Linux render node is present, falling back to CPU rendering (`GPU=off`) otherwise.

What is still a stopgap is listed in [`docs/production.md`](docs/production.md). Notably: the OS cryptex is merged into
the system volume, AMFI is patched and SIP relaxed, and memory access is slower than a native VM (4K pages vs 16K).

## Requirements

- An arm64 Linux host with PAC (Apple Silicon M1 or later in a VM: krunkit for GPU access, or tart), 4K pages, 16 GB of
  RAM (8 GB of it reserved for the hosted kernel).
- A Mac with Xcode to make the system disk and build the GPU parts.
- A macOS 27 installation (an Apple Virtualization VM disk) of your own. **No Apple binaries are in this repository or
  distributed by it**: the kexts Apple ships, the macOS system disk and its trust cache come from your own installation.

## Building and running

1. `scripts/vm-xnu-build.sh` (in the Linux VM, once): sets up the macOS-DroidVM Linux toolchain and builds XNU
   (`xnu-12377.121.6`) natively on arm64.
2. `scripts/vm-xnu-rebuild.sh`: applies `xnu-patches/`, builds the kernel and `kexts/`, and links the kernel collection
   with Apple's kexts from your macOS installation.
3. `scripts/mk-macvm-disk.sh` (on the Mac): turns a macOS VM disk made by Apple's installer into the hosted system's disk
   and copies it into the Linux VM.
4. `scripts/xnulinux-boot.sh` (in the Linux VM): builds `fki.ko` and `xnu.ko` against the running kernel, brings up the
   network (and the GPU bridge when there is a render node) and boots the hosted system. Its console is
   `scripts/xnu-console.sh`, its screen `tools/hosted/fb2png.py`, input `tools/hosted/xnu-input.py`.
5. `scripts/install-service.sh` (in the Linux VM): runs it as `xnulinux.service`, configured in `/etc/xnulinux.conf`
   (CPUs, memory, disk, GPU). On the Mac, `scripts/install-krun-agent.sh` keeps the VM itself running.
6. GPU (optional, on the Mac): `gpu/venus/build-darwin.sh` builds the hosted Vulkan driver, `gpu/xnu-cpu-metal/` the
   Metal plugin (see its README).

## Repository layout and licenses

The Linux side and the XNU side are kept apart by license and meet only at FKI. Every source file carries an
`SPDX-License-Identifier`; the license texts are in [`LICENSES/`](LICENSES).

| Path | License | What |
|---|---|---|
| `fki-ko/`, `linux/` | GPL-2.0-only | FKI: the out-of-tree module for stock kernels, and the same as an in-tree driver |
| `xnu-ko/` | APSL-2.0 | `xnu.ko`: loads XNU's kernel collection and runs it; calls Linux only through `fki_*` |
| `xnu-patches/` | APSL-2.0 | The LINUX64 machine layer and the other changes to XNU's sources, and their shared headers |
| `kexts/` | APSL-2.0 | The hosted system's kexts (CPU, disk, keystore, Metal accelerator, DRM bridge) |
| `kexts/XnuDisplay/`, `kexts/XnuEthernet/`, `kexts/XnuInput/` | BSD-2-Clause-Patent | Derived from [macOS-DroidVM](https://github.com/Droid-VM/macOS-DroidVM)'s kexts |
| `gpu/xnu-cpu-metal/` | GPL-2.0-or-later | The Metal plugin over metal2vulkan (GPL-2.0-or-later); `XnuCpuMetalShim.h` is BSD-2-Clause-Patent (from [AdrenoMetal](https://github.com/UniXNU/AdrenoMetal)) |
| `gpu/xnu-drm/` | GPL-2.0-only, MIT | `xnudrmd` (the Linux end of the DRM bridge) is GPL; the protocol header and `darwin/` (built into Mesa) are MIT |
| `gpu/venus/` | GPL-2.0-only; patches MIT | Build scripts and tests; the patches to Mesa and virglrenderer are under their upstream license (MIT) |
| `gpu/xnu-cpu-metal/patches/` | upstream's | Patches to Mesa (MIT) and metal2vulkan (GPL-2.0-or-later) |
| `scripts/`, `tools/`, `tests/`, `docs/` | GPL-2.0-only | Build, disk, boot, debugging and test tools; documentation |

`xnu.ko` is on the XNU side of the line: it runs XNU's code in its own address space, so it is APSL-2.0 like XNU, and
Linux reports it as a non-GPL module (`MODULE_LICENSE("Proprietary")`, which taints the kernel as ZFS does). It must not
include Linux headers beyond the module ABI, call Linux functions other than `fki_*`, or carry Linux code. Upstream code
(XNU, macOS-DroidVM's toolchain, Mesa, metal2vulkan, the Vulkan loader, LLVM) is fetched at pinned revisions and patched at
build time; it is never committed.

## Acknowledgements

- [macOS-DroidVM](https://github.com/Droid-VM/macOS-DroidVM) and [UniXNU](https://github.com/UniXNU): the 4K-page XNU
  base, the Linux-hosted XNU toolchain, and the display, Ethernet and input kexts these are derived from.
- [metal2vulkan](https://github.com/steelbrain/metal2vulkan), [Mesa](https://mesa3d.org) (Venus, lavapipe),
  [virglrenderer](https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/virgl/virglrenderer) and [krunkit](https://github.com/containers/krunkit).
- Apple's open-source XNU.

items.description: Distill a good Claude Code / Codex session into a skill an open-weight model can follow to reproduce the task
items.readme:
# skill-distill

A frontier model did a task well. Can an open-weight model do the same task, given the right instructions?

`skill-distill` is a skill for Claude Code or Codex (the **teacher**). You call it at the end of a good
session and name a **student**: an agent harness plus a model, for example omp with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash.
The teacher then loops:

1. reads the session and writes a skill for the student;
2. starts the student in tmux, on a fresh copy of the starting state, with the original prompt and the skill;
3. compares what the student produced with what the reference produced;
4. finds the first place the student went wrong and fixes the skill there;
5. runs again, three trials per version, until the student matches the reference.

You make the final call: the teacher shows you the reference and the student's best results side by side,
and the skill counts as done only when you accept it.

The result is two things: the reusable **operator skill** in this repo, and a **produced skill** for one task,
one model and one harness.

## Install

```
git clone https://github.com/sybil-solutions/skill-distill
ln -s "$PWD/skill-distill/skills/skill-distill" ~/.claude/skills/skill-distill    # Claude Code
ln -s "$PWD/skill-distill/skills/skill-distill" ~/.agents/skills/skill-distill    # Codex
```

Requirements: `tmux`, `git`, Python 3.10+, and the student harness installed and pointed at its model.
For web results, `pip install playwright pillow && playwright install chromium`.

## Use

At the end of a session that went well:

> distill this session into a skill for omp with deepseek-v4.1-flash on my local server

The teacher follows [`skills/skill-distill/SKILL.md`](skills/skill-distill/SKILL.md). You can watch the
students work with `tmux attach -t distill-<task>`.

## What's in it

| path | what |
|---|---|
| `skills/skill-distill/SKILL.md` | the loop the teacher follows |
| `skills/skill-distill/scripts/distill.py` | run bookkeeping: `init`, `trial`, `status`, `wait`, `evidence`, `verdict`, `ledger`, `report`, `accept` |
| `skills/skill-distill/scripts/extract_session.py` | Claude Code / Codex / omp session log → readable reference (drops system and AGENTS.md text) |
| `skills/skill-distill/scripts/capture_web.py` | serve a web app, drive it in headless Chromium, save screenshots and errors |
| `skills/skill-distill/adapters/` | one script per student harness: omp, pi, Codex, Claude Code, opencode |
| `skills/skill-distill/templates/student-skill/` | the starting shape of a produced skill |
| `examples/` | finished runs: the prompt, the produced skill, the ledger, screenshots |

## Rules the teacher follows

- The student gets the reference's prompt verbatim, a clean starting state, and the skill. Nothing else:
  the student harness's own global context files and skills are turned off where the harness allows it.
- The skill may not contain the reference's finished output or a script that writes it. It teaches the
  steps, decisions, traps and checks; short snippets only where the student can't get a part right otherwise.
- Three trials per skill version. One lucky run proves nothing.
- Checks are tested on the reference first. A check that fails on the reference is a broken check.
- Raw session logs stay in `runs/`, which is git-ignored: they contain your machine's paths and context.

## Adapters

| harness | status |
|---|---|
| omp (oh-my-pi) | tested |
| Codex CLI | tested as the teacher; as a student needs a provider in `STUDENT_ARGS` |
| Claude Code | written; open models need `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` to an Anthropic-compatible server |
| pi | written, untested |
| opencode | written, untested; its JSON log has no parser in `extract_session.py` yet |

## License

MIT

items.readme:
# Agentic Attack Detections

[![validate](https://github.com/ThreatDefence/agentic-attack-detections/actions/workflows/validate.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/ThreatDefence/agentic-attack-detections/actions/workflows/validate.yml)
[![release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/ThreatDefence/agentic-attack-detections)](https://github.com/ThreatDefence/agentic-attack-detections/releases)
[![license](https://img.shields.io/github/license/ThreatDefence/agentic-attack-detections)](LICENSE)

Open-source detection rules, hunting queries and indicators for security teams. They cover agentic attack frameworks: tools that hand an intrusion to AI agents, which plan, run real attack tools and keep going until they reach a goal.

Free to use under the MIT license. Fixes, false-positive reports and new indicators are welcome.

## What is here

- **Framework folders.** ARTEX and its AntiFox fork, Cairn, PentAGI, HexStrike, CyberStrikeAI, Strix, Hermes Agent, Agent Zero, RedAmon, Xalgorix and Pentest Swarm AI. Each folder is built from a review of the framework's source code and the public reporting on its use.
- **Shared behaviors.** Rules for what these frameworks have in common, whatever the tool or the model behind it.
- **Indicators and feeds.** One CSV of 572 sourced indicators, and the feeds generated from it.
- **Exposed consoles.** A dated list of addresses where one of these consoles answers on the internet, in [`exposure/`](exposure), with a [count per framework](#exposed-consoles). It is a record of what is exposed, not a detection feed.

Formats: KQL for Microsoft Sentinel and Defender XDR, Sigma, Suricata, Zeek, YARA and STIX 2.1, plus WAF rules for Cloudflare, AWS WAF and Azure WAF. Splunk and Elastic are covered by a Splunk app and Elastic rules for ARTEX, and by Sigma conversions for everything else.

## Try it in a minute

With Suricata installed, run the ARTEX rules over the sample capture in this repository:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/ThreatDefence/agentic-attack-detections
cd agentic-attack-detections
mkdir -p out
suricata -r frameworks/artex/tests/artex-sample.pcap -S frameworks/artex/suricata/artex.rules -l out -k none
cat out/fast.log
```

You should see alerts such as:

```text
[1:3800001:1] TD ARTEX user agent artex-<role>/1.0
[1:3800020:1] TD ARTEX placeholder probe path
[1:3800023:2] TD Unsigned alg none JWT in URI
```

The capture is test traffic written from the framework source code and published reports. It is not a recorded intrusion.

## Start here

| You have | Do this |
|---|---|
| Microsoft Sentinel | Upload `feeds/sentinel-watchlist.csv` as a watchlist with the alias `AGENTIC_IOCs` and the search key `value`. Import the analytics rules from `frameworks/*/sentinel/analytics/` and `behaviors/sentinel/analytics/`. Run the hunts in each folder's `hunting-order.md` order |
| Defender XDR | Run the hunts from `frameworks/*/sentinel/hunting/` in advanced hunting. They work where the tables exist |
| Suricata | Add the `.rules` files from `frameworks/*/suricata/` and `behaviors/suricata/`. HTTP rules need cleartext or decrypted traffic. DNS and TLS SNI rules work on encrypted traffic |
| Zeek | Install the behaviors package with `zkg install https://github.com/ThreatDefence/agentic-attack-detections` (or load `behaviors/zeek/agentic-behaviors/` by path), set `server_nets` to your server ranges ([setup](behaviors/zeek/README.md)), load `frameworks/artex/zeek/artex/`, and feed `frameworks/*/zeek/intel/*.intel` to the Intel framework |
| YARA | Scan container layers, home folders, `/tmp` and web roots with `frameworks/*/yara/` |
| Any SIEM with Sigma | Convert `frameworks/*/sigma/` and `behaviors/sigma/` with `sigma convert`, or take the conversions in [`generated/`](generated) |
| Splunk or Elastic | The ARTEX folder has a Splunk app and Elastic rules. For the other frameworks use [`generated/`](generated) |
| A WAF: Cloudflare, AWS WAF or Azure WAF | Deploy the rules in [`waf/`](waf): framework user agents, probe markers and unsigned JWT probes to block, and reported addresses to challenge. A WAF is optional. It adds blocking at the edge to the detections, it doesn't replace them |
| A threat intelligence platform | Import `feeds/stix2.1-bundle.json`, or the per-framework lists in `feeds/by-framework/` |

## Coverage

| | KQL hunts | Sentinel analytics | Sigma | Suricata | YARA | Zeek | Indicators |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| [ARTEX](frameworks/artex) | 31 | 7 | 36 | 43 | 4 | script, intel | 246 |
| [Cairn](frameworks/cairn) | 6 | 2 | 3 | 26 | 6 | intel | 73 |
| [PentAGI](frameworks/pentagi) | 5 | 2 | 3 | 10 | 3 | intel | 39 |
| [HexStrike](frameworks/hexstrike) | 4 | 2 | 3 | 7 | 3 | intel | 22 |
| [CyberStrikeAI](frameworks/cyberstrikeai) | 5 | 2 | 7 | 11 | 4 | intel | 73 |
| [Strix](frameworks/strix) | 3 | 1 | 3 | 5 | 3 | intel | 49 |
| [Hermes Agent](frameworks/hermes) | 4 | 2 | 3 | 7 | 4 | intel | 75 |
| [Agent Zero](frameworks/agent-zero) | 2 | | 1 | 3 | 1 | intel | 8 |
| [RedAmon](frameworks/redamon) | 3 | | 3 | 10 | 1 | intel | 19 |
| [Xalgorix](frameworks/xalgorix) | 3 | | 3 | 10 | 1 | intel | 22 |
| [Pentest Swarm AI](frameworks/pentestswarm) | 3 | | 3 | 11 | 1 | intel | 15 |
| [Shared behaviors](behaviors) | 9 | 2 | 5 | 16 | | package | |

Suricata counts are hand-written rules; each framework also has address rules generated from its indicators. Some indicators belong to more than one framework. ARTEX also has a Splunk app, Elastic rules and ES\|QL queries, and an osquery pack.

## Frameworks

| Framework | What it is | Seen in |
|---|---|---|
| [ARTEX](frameworks/artex) | Go planner and worker agents with a web console. AntiFox is the same code renamed | Storm-0940, Storm-3358, VAPOR PANDA and criminal groups, against Microsoft 365, Okta, AWS, Azure, web applications and Active Directory |
| [Cairn](frameworks/cairn) | Python engine that drives Claude Code, Codex and Pi coding agents in Kali containers | Online retailers, payment sites, Japanese web applications and WSUS servers |
| [PentAGI](frameworks/pentagi) | Go multi-agent platform that runs Kali tools in a container per engagement | Intrusions GTIG and Mandiant reported since August 2026, and a PaperCut exploitation operator's infrastructure |
| [HexStrike](frameworks/hexstrike) | Python MCP server that gives any AI assistant about 150 security tools over an unauthenticated API | NetScaler exploitation discussion in 2025, and intrusions GTIG and Mandiant reported |
| [CyberStrikeAI](frameworks/cyberstrikeai) | Go operator console whose agents run about 90 tools, with its own implants, C2 listeners and webshell manager | FortiGate mass-exploitation infrastructure, an AWS intrusion, and education organizations in Africa and Latin America |
| [Strix](frameworks/strix) | Python AI pentest agent that runs teams of agents in a Kali sandbox, on any model | The retail card-theft campaign Gambit reported, where it found the flaws Cairn exploited |
| [Hermes Agent](frameworks/hermes) | A legitimate general-purpose agent turned into an attack console: approvals off, a bundled jailbreak skill, red-team personas | The Gambit retail operator, the Carbonato Docker botnet, and Thailand's Ministry of Finance |
| [Agent Zero](frameworks/agent-zero) | General-purpose agent in a Kali container with a built-in hacker profile and an open web UI | Threat-actor experimentation GTIG reported, with no published indicators |
| [RedAmon](frameworks/redamon) | Self-hosted penetration testing platform: a web console, a recon pipeline and an agent that exploits from a Kali sandbox with Metasploit | No public report of use in an attack. Covered from its source code |
| [Xalgorix](frameworks/xalgorix) | Go binary with a web dashboard whose agent tests web applications and APIs without approval steps and re-exploits each finding | No public report of use in an attack. Covered from its source code |
| [Pentest Swarm AI](frameworks/pentestswarm) | Go command-line tool that runs recon, exploit and report agents over about 40 security tools | No public report of use in an attack. Covered from its source code |

Each folder has a README, the hunts and rules, and a `source-code-signals.md` that explains what the framework leaves behind and where in its code each signal comes from.

## Exposed consoles

Hosts on the internet that serve the web console of each framework, found in internet-wide scan data with the fingerprints the rules here use: favicons, page titles, page text that survives a rename, and certificates.

<!-- exposed-consoles:start -->
An active host is one seen in the seven days to November 23, 2026.

| Framework | Active hosts | Seen in 30 days |
|---|---|---|
| [ARTEX](frameworks/artex) and AntiFox | 2,117 | 2,816 |
| [Hermes Agent](frameworks/hermes) | 1,016 | 2,192 |
| [CyberStrikeAI](frameworks/cyberstrikeai) | 799 | 1,188 |
| [PentAGI](frameworks/pentagi) | 329 | 500 |
| [Agent Zero](frameworks/agent-zero) | 116 | 175 |
| [HexStrike](frameworks/hexstrike) | 25 | 30 |
| [RedAmon](frameworks/redamon) | 20 | 34 |
| [Cairn](frameworks/cairn) | 17 | 30 |
| [Xalgorix](frameworks/xalgorix) | 6 | 13 |
| [Strix](frameworks/strix) | 5 | 12 |
| [Pentest Swarm AI](frameworks/pentestswarm) | 0 | 0 |
| All, each host counted once | 4,275 | 6,715 |
<!-- exposed-consoles:end -->

- An exposed console is not proof of an attack. Researchers, students and security teams run these tools, and some hosts are decoys.
- One network holds about a fifth of the CyberStrikeAI hosts and more than a third of the PentAGI hosts. That looks like one mass deployment or a set of decoys, not that many operators ([#21](https://github.com/ThreatDefence/agentic-attack-detections/issues/21)).
- Hermes Agent and Agent Zero are general-purpose agents, so their numbers count exposed agents, not attack consoles. Hermes is counted on its default port only.
- Consoles served by host name only, or on a port that has not been scanned, are not counted.

The addresses, with the port and the fingerprint that found each one, are in [`exposure/consoles.csv`](exposure/consoles.csv). The counts of every snapshot are kept in [`exposure/history.csv`](exposure/history.csv), so the numbers can be followed over time.

## Behaviors shared by agentic frameworks

[`behaviors/`](behaviors) holds rules that do not depend on any one framework.

| Behavior | Rules |
|---|---|
| An attack tool started under an AI agent CLI (Claude Code, Qwen Code, Kimi CLI, Codex, opencode, Hermes, Cairn's workers), found from the process tree | KQL hunt, Sentinel analytics rule, Sigma |
| Servers calling AI model APIs: Chinese models (DeepSeek, Qwen, GLM, Kimi, MiniMax, Doubao), gateways such as OpenRouter, and Western APIs | KQL hunt, Sigma, Zeek |
| An AI agent's page reader on your application next to attack traffic from the same address | KQL hunt, Sigma, Suricata, Zeek |
| One site probed through hundreds of rotating proxy addresses | KQL hunt, Zeek |
| Configuration and backup file theft, and probes of WSUS administration services | KQL hunt, Sentinel analytics rule, Sigma, Suricata, Zeek |
| Kerberos user enumeration and SMB or WinRM fan-out from one address | KQL hunt, Zeek |
| A server calling back to the address that was probing it | KQL hunt, Suricata (PentAGI worker ports), Zeek |
| AWS credentials used at machine speed from one outside address | KQL hunt |
| Servers looking up out-of-band testing domains (interactsh, Burp Collaborator, dnslog.cn), which means a blind payload ran on them | KQL hunt, Sigma, Suricata, Zeek |

The ARTEX folder also carries behavior hunts that apply to every framework: user agent family bursts (hunt 17), web and database services starting shells (hunt 11), servers calling webhook and tunnel services (hunt 12), scripts written into web folders (hunt 13), and Kerberoasting, DCSync and WinRM fan-out (hunt 16).

## Indicators and feeds

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| [`iocs/indicators.csv`](iocs/indicators.csv) | 572 indicators. Each row has its source, confidence, a review date for addresses and the framework it belongs to. This file is the single source for every feed |
| [`feeds/`](feeds) | Generated from the CSV: a STIX 2.1 bundle, a Sentinel watchlist, and plain lists of addresses, domains, URLs, user agents and hashes. The plain lists carry medium and high confidence rows only. Low confidence rows, which include legitimate services such as AI model APIs, need their context, so they stay in the CSV, the watchlist and the STIX bundle. [`feeds/by-framework/`](feeds/by-framework) has the lists per framework |
| [`generated/`](generated) | Every Sigma rule converted to Splunk SPL, Sentinel and Defender XDR KQL, and Elastic ES\|QL and Lucene. [`SUMMARY.md`](generated/SUMMARY.md) shows which rule converted to which backend |
| [`waf/`](waf) | Cloudflare, AWS WAF and Azure WAF rules built from [`waf/signatures.yaml`](waf/signatures.yaml) and the CSV. The [README](waf/README.md) covers when a WAF helps and how to deploy |
| [`exposure/`](exposure) | Addresses where one of these consoles answers on the internet, with the fingerprint that found each one. A record of what is exposed, kept out of the feeds above. `tools/exposure_snapshot.py` rebuilds it |
| [`tools/`](tools) | Feed builder, WAF builder, release file builder, Sigma converter and validator |
| [`docs/`](docs) | [Adding a framework](docs/adding-a-framework.md) |

Each framework folder also has a Zeek intel file and Suricata address rules, generated from the same CSV.

### Downloads

Each [release](https://github.com/ThreatDefence/agentic-attack-detections/releases) carries the same content as ready-made files. These links always point at the newest release:

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| [`agentic-attack-detections.rules`](https://github.com/ThreatDefence/agentic-attack-detections/releases/latest/download/agentic-attack-detections.rules) | Every Suricata rule in one file |
| [`agentic-attack-detections-yara.zip`](https://github.com/ThreatDefence/agentic-attack-detections/releases/latest/download/agentic-attack-detections-yara.zip) | The YARA rules, one file per framework |
| [`agentic-attack-detections-stix2.1.json`](https://github.com/ThreatDefence/agentic-attack-detections/releases/latest/download/agentic-attack-detections-stix2.1.json) | The STIX 2.1 bundle |
| [`agentic-attack-detections-indicators.zip`](https://github.com/ThreatDefence/agentic-attack-detections/releases/latest/download/agentic-attack-detections-indicators.zip) | `iocs/indicators.csv` and every feed |
| [`agentic-attack-detections-waf.zip`](https://github.com/ThreatDefence/agentic-attack-detections/releases/latest/download/agentic-attack-detections-waf.zip) | The WAF rules for Cloudflare, AWS WAF and Azure WAF |
| [`SHA256SUMS.txt`](https://github.com/ThreatDefence/agentic-attack-detections/releases/latest/download/SHA256SUMS.txt) | SHA-256 of each file |

To keep the Suricata rules current with `suricata-update`:

```bash
suricata-update add-source agentic-attack-detections https://github.com/ThreatDefence/agentic-attack-detections/releases/latest/download/agentic-attack-detections.rules
suricata-update
```

## How the rules are built and checked

- **From source.** A signature string comes from the framework's code at a named commit, or from a report that published it. `source-code-signals.md` gives the file and line.
- **From reports.** Every indicator names the report it came from, and each value was checked against that report.
- **Tested.** Each Suricata rule has a test flow and a near miss. Sigma rules are run against test events, and hunts and analytics rules against sample rows in Microsoft's Kusto emulator, where cases have been written: [`tests/sigma/`](tests/sigma) and [`tests/kql/`](tests/kql) have the formats, and new cases are welcome. Every KQL query is parsed with Microsoft's parser and its columns checked. The Zeek packages run against test captures. CI runs the validator and the Suricata, Sigma and KQL tests on every push.
- **Run on real data.** Version 2.7.0 was run over 30 days of production telemetry to remove rules that could not fire and to quiet rules that were noisy.

No rule has been tested against a captured intrusion. Treat every rule as experimental until it has run on your own data.

## Confidence

| Level | Meaning | How to use it |
|---|---|---|
| High | Specific to a framework or its campaigns: its user agents, command lines, paths, prompt strings, probe artifacts, reported C2 and skimmer domains, file hashes | Alert |
| Medium | Seen in a framework's activity but changeable or shared: reported addresses, generic agent user agents, prompt text shared with similar tools | Alert after baselining, or hunt |
| Low | Common or legitimate: AI model APIs, request-collection services, agent CLI user agents, hosting ASNs, proxy providers | Context for another finding only |

Addresses from cloud and VPS providers are reassigned. Every address has a `review_by` date 180 days after it was reported. Addresses past that date are left out of the plain lists, the Zeek intel files and the Suricata address rules; they stay in the CSV and the STIX bundle as history. Check before you block.

## Testing

```bash
pip install -r tools/requirements.txt
python3 tools/validate.py                              # Sigma, KQL, ES|QL, TOML, Splunk, Suricata SIDs, YARA, Zeek, osquery, feeds
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests/feeds            # indicator confidence, expiry and SID policy
python3 tests/sigma/run_tests.py                       # Sigma rules against test events
python3 tests/kql/run_tests.py                         # hunts and analytics against sample rows; needs the Kusto emulator
python3 tools/convert.py                               # regenerate generated/
python3 tools/build_waf.py                             # regenerate waf/
python3 tests/waf/run_tests.py                         # offline checks of the WAF rules on every platform
python3 tools/build_release.py                         # build the release downloads into dist/
python3 tests/suricata/run_tests.py                    # one flow per Suricata rule; needs suricata and openssl
bash frameworks/artex/tests/run_network_tests.sh       # needs zeek and suricata on the PATH
bash behaviors/zeek/tests/run_tests.sh                 # needs zeek on the PATH
```

`validate.py` checks KQL with Microsoft's parser when `dotnet` is installed, and Zeek scripts when `zeek` is.
